transcript.content: Hello, I'm glad to meet you today. What brings you in to see me?

My thoughts feel all jumbled and I can’t keep my words or plans straight anymore, even for simple tasks I’ve done for years. It’s just gotten to the point where I can't even manage my daily routine, and I'm really struggling.
Along with these difficulties with your thoughts, have you also been feeling persistently down, sad, or lost interest in activities you usually enjoy?
No, I wouldn't say I feel depressed or down like that. It's more that my mood is either way too high and wired, or I'm just incredibly frustrated and angry because my mind is constantly buzzing.
Do these difficulties with your thinking and organizing your routine happen only during the times when your mood is very high and wired, or do they persist even when your mood is stable?

Even during the quieter weeks when my mood feels more flat and I'm not rushing around, those jumbled thoughts and the feeling of being watched don't go away. I still hear that man's voice whispering to me even when I'm not in those high, wired phases.
Have these voices or the feeling of being watched ever lasted for two weeks or more at a time when your mood was completely stable and not high or wired?

Yes, they have. Even during a couple of quieter weeks when my mood felt flat and I wasn't rushing around, I still heard that man's voice telling me they were going to take my husband away. I also stayed completely convinced that the hospital and my boss were secretly watching and judging me during that time.

Looking back at the entire time you've struggled with these jumbled thoughts and voices, would you say those high, wired mood phases have been present for most of that time, or only for a small part of it?

Yes, looking back over this whole stretch since my husband's health got bad, those high and wired phases have been present for most of the time. I'm usually either in that revved-up, can't-sit-still mode or just coming down from it, with only very short spells where I feel like my old steady self.
During those times when you feel highly wired and revved up, do you find that you need much less sleep than usual—perhaps only a few hours—but still feel full of energy?

Yes, that's exactly what happens. Most nights during those phases I only sleep about two or three hours, but instead of feeling exhausted, I wake up feeling completely wired and full of energy. It feels like I don't even need sleep at all.

latest_inference.note: The patient describes both prominent manic symptoms (elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, high energy) and schizophrenic symptoms (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, thought disorganization). The psychotic symptoms persist for at least two weeks in the absence of mood symptoms, which supports a schizoaffective presentation (F25) over bipolar disorder. Additionally, because the manic phases have been present for most of the total duration of the illness, F25 is more appropriate than F20, though F20 remains a differential. Sufficient evidence has been gathered to finalize the diagnostic candidates.

inference_history.note: The patient reports prominent manic-like symptoms ('high and wired' phases) present for most of the duration of the illness, alongside persistent psychotic symptoms (voices, delusions of being watched) that continue for at least two weeks during periods of stable mood. This independent persistence of psychosis rules out a primary mood disorder with psychotic features (like F31.2). The differential remains between Schizoaffective disorder (F25), which is highly likely given the dominance of the mood episodes, and Schizophrenia (F20). I will ask about other manic symptoms (e.g., sleep, energy, grandiosity) to further characterize the affective component.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits prominent symptoms of both schizophrenia (auditory hallucinations, persecutory delusions, and disorganized thinking) and mania (elated/wired mood, decreased need for sleep, and psychomotor agitation). The psychotic symptoms persisted for at least two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, but the manic episodes have been present for a substantial portion of the total duration of the illness, which is characteristic of Schizoaffective disorder (F25) rather than Schizophrenia (F20).
